blocks.text: A roadside bread seller pays retail prices for flour, borrows from a cooperative at high interest and advertises by shouting. A national bakery buys flour by the tanker, borrows from a bank at prime rate and advertises on television. Both sell bread. Only one of them can sell it cheaply — and the reason is scale.

blocks.markdown:
**Economies of scale** are the reductions in average cost per unit that a firm enjoys as its scale of production expands. **Diseconomies of scale** are the increases in average cost that set in when a firm grows beyond a certain size.

They explain the U shape of the long-run average cost curve: costs per unit fall as the firm grows, reach a minimum at the **optimum size**, and then rise.

blocks.title: Internal and external economies
blocks.text: INTERNAL economies arise from the growth of the individual FIRM itself and are enjoyed by that firm alone. EXTERNAL economies arise from the growth of the whole INDUSTRY or the area in which it is located, and are shared by every firm in it. This distinction is the single most heavily examined point in the topic.

rows: Large, specialised machinery becomes worth installing, and larger vessels or plants cost less per unit of capacity
Specialist managers can be employed for finance, marketing and production, and their salaries are spread over more output
Bulk buying attracts discounts, and one advertising campaign covers a far larger volume of sales
Large firms borrow more easily, at lower interest, and can raise capital by issuing shares and debentures
Output, markets and suppliers can be diversified, so one failure does not sink the firm
A research department can be afforded, and its cost is spread across large output
blocks.caption: Internal economies of scale

items: **External economies** — a pool of skilled labour trained by the industry, specialist subsidiary firms supplying parts and repairs, shared infrastructure such as roads, power and water provided because the industry is there, trade journals and shared technical information, and a reputation that attracts buyers to the area.

**Internal diseconomies** — management becomes stretched beyond an effective span of control, decisions are delayed by layers of bureaucracy, industrial relations deteriorate as workers become remote from managers, and a plant can grow too large to run efficiently.
**External diseconomies** — congestion and higher transport costs, rising rents and land prices, competition among firms bidding up local wages, pressure on power and water supply, and pollution.

blocks.markdown:
### Localisation and the location of industry

**Localisation** is the concentration of a particular industry in a particular area, and it is the main source of external economies. **Delocalisation** is the deliberate dispersal of industry to other areas, usually through government incentives, to spread employment and reduce congestion.

A firm chooses its location by weighing:

- **Nearness to raw materials**, which dominates where the material is bulky or perishable. Nigeria's cement works at Ewekoro, Sokoto and Obajana sit on limestone deposits.
- **Nearness to the market**, which dominates where the finished product is bulky, fragile or perishable — hence breweries and bottling plants near large cities.
- **Power supply** — reliable electricity or gas.
- **Labour supply**, both its quantity and its skills.
- **Transport and communication** links, including ports for exporters.
- **Water supply**, critical for breweries, textiles and tanneries.
- **Availability of land** at a reasonable price for expansion.
- **Government policy**, such as tax holidays, industrial estates and free trade zones.
- **Climate and security**.

blocks.title: Sorting economies into internal and external
blocks.prompt: A furniture firm in a town where furniture making has grown rapidly reports four cost savings: (i) it installed an automated cutting machine; (ii) a technical college in the town now trains upholsterers; (iii) it obtained a bank loan at 3 percentage points below its old rate; (iv) a specialist varnish supplier has opened nearby. Classify each and give the type where internal.

steps.text: Ask of each item: does the saving come from the growth of THIS firm, or from the growth of the industry and the area?
(i) The automated machine is affordable because this firm's own output is large. Internal — a technical economy.
(ii) The technical college trains workers for every furniture firm in the town, not just this one. External.
(iii) The cheaper loan reflects this firm's own size and creditworthiness. Internal — a financial economy.
(iv) The varnish supplier was drawn by the whole industry's presence and serves all of it. External.
So two internal economies, technical and financial, and two external economies arising from localisation.

blocks.answer: (i) internal, technical; (ii) external; (iii) internal, financial; (iv) external

blocks.title: Define the optimum firm carefully
blocks.text: The optimum firm is the one operating at the size where long-run average cost is at its minimum — not the largest firm, and not the most profitable one. A firm can be highly profitable while producing above or below optimum size.

points: Economies of scale reduce average cost per unit as the scale of production grows.
Internal economies come from the growth of the firm itself; external economies come from the growth of the industry or locality.
Internal economies are technical, managerial, marketing, financial, risk-bearing and research-based.
Diseconomies of scale set in through stretched management, bureaucracy, poor industrial relations, congestion and rising local costs.
The optimum firm operates where long-run average cost is lowest.
Localisation concentrates an industry in one area and generates external economies; location decisions weigh raw materials, market, power, labour, transport, water, land and government policy.
